interest: This file is particularly valuable for historians studying the aftermath of World War II in East Asia, capturing both Allied negotiations over Japanese reparations and the turbulent reintegration of Taiwan (Formosa) into Nationalist China. Most notably, Ambassador J. Leighton Stewart's candid letter reflects U.S. diplomatic deliberations following the February 28 Incident, evaluating George H. Kerr's assessments of native discontent against mainland administrative ineptitude and the National Resources Commission's centralizing grip. The correspondence illuminates early Cold War strategy, showing how American officials sought to stabilize Taiwan's economy and counter communist influence through technocratic American industrial advisers (such as George S. Armstrong) and private American investment (such as Reynolds Aluminum) rather than overt political intervention. Furthermore, the cross-filing of 894A.50A material within the 894.50A Japan decimal series illustrates the State Department's ongoing administrative association of Taiwan's economic structure with its former Japanese colonial apparatus.
overview: This State Department file (decimal file 894.50A and 894A.50A) spans December 1946 to May 1948 and focuses on economic advisers and post-World War II economic reorganization in Japan and Formosa (Taiwan). The file opens with a December 1946 communication from Edwin M. Martin of the Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs to Australian Far Eastern Commission delegate Major James Plimsoll concerning the potential recruitment of Australian economic and engineering experts for reparations work in Japan. The remainder of the file, dated April and May 1948, consists of high-level correspondence between U.S. Ambassador to China J. Leighton Stewart and Director of Far Eastern Affairs W. Walton Butterworth regarding political and economic unrest in Formosa following retrocession. Stewart analyzes the roots of Taiwanese dissatisfaction, discusses George H. Kerr's reporting, assesses Governor Wei Tao-min and the National Resources Commission, and strongly recommends recruiting an American industrial adviser—specifically proposing engineering consultant George S. Armstrong—to foster industrial rehabilitation and encourage private American capital investment, a proposal Butterworth advises should officially originate from Chinese authorities.

subfiles.about: Interim reply to Australia regarding an offer to provide economic and engineering specialists for Japanese reparations work.
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.summary: Edwin M. Martin writes to Major J. Plimsoll in an interim response concerning Australia's generous offer to supply economic and engineering experts for reparations work in Japan. Martin explains that a committee appointed by Secretary of War Robert P. Patterson is presently authorized solely to discuss the recruitment of competent trained personnel. Until those deliberations conclude, no definitive acceptance can be made, though Martin expresses appreciation for Australia's patience and promises an update within a month.
subfiles.title: Letter from Edwin M. Martin to Major J. Plimsoll on Australian Experts for Japanese Reparations
subfiles.to: Major J. Plimsoll, Australian Delegate, Far Eastern Commission

subfiles.about: Detailed assessment of unrest in Formosa and a recommendation to recruit an American industrial adviser to guide economic rehabilitation.
subfiles.from: J. Leighton Stewart, U.S. Ambassador to China
subfiles.summary: Ambassador J. Leighton Stewart responds to W. Walton Butterworth's letter regarding a memorandum by George H. Kerr, confirming Kerr's reporting of severe discontent and incipient revolt in Formosa while attributing the problems primarily to mainland administrative inexperience, excessive centralization by the National Resources Commission, and disruptions to the former Japanese colonial economic structure. Stewart argues that the most effective remedy is economic development rather than overt political reform, endorsing the selection of George S. Armstrong as a high-grade American industrial adviser to assist Governor Wei Tao-min and Chiang Kai-shek. He emphasizes that promoting industrial stabilization and joint Chinese-American ventures like Reynolds Aluminum will foster political security, improve living conditions, and strengthen the Nationalist government against communism.
subfiles.title: Letter from Ambassador J. Leighton Stewart to W. Walton Butterworth on Conditions in Formosa and Proposed Industrial Adviser
subfiles.to: W. Walton Butterworth, Director, Office of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Instructions advising that Chinese authorities must formally initiate the request for an American industrial adviser before the U.S. assists.
subfiles.from: George C. Marshall, Secretary of State (drafted by W. Walton Butterworth)
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State George C. Marshall transmits a confidential telegram drafted by W. Walton Butterworth to Ambassador J. Leighton Stewart in Nanking in response to Stewart's April 26 letter. The Department instructs that regarding the recruitment of industrial consultant George S. Armstrong, it is diplomatic policy and preference that the Chinese authorities take the initial formal action to request the adviser. Once Chinese leaders take this step, the United States Government will gladly render every appropriate assistance.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Secretary of State Marshall (Butterworth) to Embassy Nanking on Industrial Adviser for Formosa
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Nanking (for Ambassador J. Leighton Stewart)
